summary: Solid, family-friendly core exists. Consistent across a Mexican government book (INPI 2022), a Yucatan research-centre note (CICY), a Yucatec dictionary gloss (Bolles via FAMSI), Wikipedia and several regional articles: the ceiba (Ceiba pentandra, English kapok) is a huge, thorny, long-lived tree called ya'axche' ('green tree' or 'first tree') in Yucatec Maya. In Maya cosmology it links three levels: roots reach the underworld (Xibalba), the trunk stands on the earth where people live, and the crown reaches the sky. Because of this it is treated as a sacred tree; in many Maya towns a ceiba still stands in the middle of the plaza, people treat its place with respect, and (per INPI) hold a ceremony to thank it before one is cut. It also gives shade, kapok fibre for pillows, timber and traditional medicine. Merida's government (2024) is planting ceibas in the Plaza Grande as the tree that connects sky, earth and underworld. Safe story spine: a village plaza, a giant ceiba, children playing in its shade, a grandmother explaining the name and the three levels, and why everyone respects the tree. Avoid Xtabay, creation myths, the end-of-times prophecy and the colour/direction meanings.
facts: The ceiba (Ceiba pentandra; English name kapok) is a very tall tree native to the Americas. Typical heights quoted are about 20-40 m; some reach 60 m or more (Wikipedia gives a laser-verified maximum of 60.4 m; INPI says 60-70 m in exceptional cases; Mexico Desconocido says up to 70 m documented). Trunks can be several metres wide and trees can live for centuries (INPI: more than 500 years). [INPI 2022; Mexico Desconocido; Wikipedia Ceiba pentandra]
The trunk and big branches can be covered in large thorns/spines, and the huge buttress roots stand out above the ground. [INPI 2022; Wikipedia Ceiba pentandra; mayan.org]

In Yucatec Maya the ceiba is ya'axche' (variants: yaaxche', yaxche, ya'ax che'). Meaning: 'green tree' or 'first tree' (ya'ax = green/first + che' = tree). The Bolles Yucatec dictionary (FAMSI) glosses 'Yax-che. Ceiba pentandra ... Lit. first tree or green tree.' INPI also glosses it 'arbol verde'; Por Esto and mayan.org agree. [FAMSI/Bolles; INPI 2022; Por Esto 2026; mayan.org]

Core meaning: the Maya cosmos has three levels - sky, earth, underworld - and the ceiba connects them. Roots reach down to the underworld (Xibalba), the trunk stands on the surface where people live, and branches/crown reach up to the sky (heavens). INPI: 'las ramas y hojas superiores ... el mundo espiritual; sus raices, el inframundo o Xibalba; y su tronco ... el mundo en donde todos nosotros vivimos.' [INPI 2022; Por Esto 2026; Mexico Desconocido; CICY (sky and underworld); HistoricalMX; mayan.org; Wikipedia Mesoamerican world tree (axis mundi connecting underworld, sky and terrestrial realm)]

The ceiba is called the centre/'navel' and axis of the universe, and a 'tree of life'. Qualities attached to it: life, permanence, greatness, goodness, strength, unity. [INPI 2022; Mexico Desconocido; Yucatan Today]

Scholars read Classic-period art at Palenque (Pakal's sarcophagus lid, Temple of the Cross tablets) as showing a world tree, though Wikipedia words it as 'considered a possible representation'. The world-tree idea is therefore old, but see cautions on the term yax cheel cab. [Wikipedia Mesoamerican world tree; mayan.org]

Respect: INPI says the place where a ceiba stands is considered sacred and deserving of great respect, and that before cutting a ceiba, people hold ceremonies thanking the tree for lending its life. Por Esto says many communities avoided cutting it. [INPI 2022; Por Esto 2026]

Plaza: INPI says that even today in many Maya towns and communities the ceiba's place is the central place of their plazas, serving as roof/shelter, medicine and food. Por Esto says many communities placed it in the centre of plazas or ceremonial spaces; Yucatan Today says it was always planted in plaza centres (stated more absolutely). Consistent core: 'in many villages the ceiba stands in the middle of the plaza.' [INPI 2022; Por Esto 2026; Yucatan Today]

Gifts of the tree: wide shade; kapok fibre from the seed pods used to stuff pillows and mattresses; wood for houses and canoes; bark and resin in traditional medicine for wounds, toothache, burns and more; seeds are edible cooked or roasted (INPI only). [INPI 2022; CICY Herbario 2010; Wikipedia Ceiba pentandra; Por Esto 2026]

Modern Yucatan: ceibas are planted ornamentally in parks and medians in Merida (CICY, 2010). The Yucatan state government's 2024 Plaza Grande planting plan puts ceibas at the centre of the park's four trapezoid areas and describes the ceiba as 'el arbol sagrado de la vida que conecta el cielo, la tierra y el inframundo'. A monument to the Xtabay stands in Merida. [CICY Herbario 2010; Posta 21 Aug 2024 reporting Gobierno de Yucatan]

Four directional ceibas: a widely repeated account says four ceibas stand at the four corners of the world holding up the sky - red east, black west, yellow south, white north - with the great ceiba at the centre. The colours agree across INPI, Yucatan Today and Wikipedia's general description; the meanings of each colour differ or appear in one source only. [INPI 2022; Yucatan Today; Wikipedia Mesoamerican world tree]

Folk belief: the Xtabay legend is a living oral tradition tied to the ceiba - a spirit said to wait near the ceiba and lure people who walk alone at night. It is folklore, not part of the ancient cosmology, and versions differ (see variants). [INPI 2022; Wikipedia Xtabay; Yucatan Today; CICY 2010]

Poetic images in INPI's opening poem (wind passing through its branches makes sacred music; quetzals and hummingbirds in its upper part; the tree gives shade, food, shelter and medicine) are lyrical, usable as imagery but not as 'facts'. [INPI 2022]
variants: Name spelling: ya'axche' (modern Yucatec, apostrophes), Yaaxche (INPI), yaxche / Yax-che (Bolles dictionary, Spanish and popular sources), Ya'ax che' / yaax che' (some tourism pages), Yaxche (mayan.org, HistoricalMX). All mean the ceiba.
Name meaning: 'green tree' (INPI, Bolles, mayan.org, Por Esto) or 'first tree' (Bolles, mayan.org, Por Esto). Both are given together in the dictionary: use 'green tree / first tree'.

Other world-tree names: wacah chan (Classic Maya; mayan.org glosses it Six-Sky-Tree), yax imix che (Wikipedia, depends on language), yax cheel cab ('first tree of the world', Itza, recorded 1696). Not needed in a beginner story.
Number of heavens: Yucatan Today and Por Esto say the branches reach 13 heavens; INPI and the government communique only say 'the sky'. Prefer 'the sky'.

Directional ceibas: popular sources (Yucatan Today, others) attribute the four coloured trees to the Popol Vuh; this is unconfirmed, and the Popol Vuh is a K'iche' text rather than Yucatec. Colours are consistent (red E, black W, yellow S, white N) but INPI alone gives each colour a meaning (north white = ancestors' paradise, south yellow = maize deities, east red = rain/life/youth, west black = place of the dead). Some blogs list other colours (e.g. green centre).

Plaza placement strength: INPI 'in many Maya towns, still the central place of their plazas'; Por Esto 'many communities'; Yucatan Today 'always planted in the centre of plazas'; mayan.org 'traditionally planted in the centre of villages and never cut down'. Use the hedged 'in many villages'.

Cutting: mayan.org says never cut down; INPI says it is cut only after a thanking ceremony; Por Esto says many communities avoided cutting. Use 'people treat it with great respect and ask or thank it before cutting', not 'never cut'.

Xtabay: INPI version - sisters Utz-colel (proud, cold) and Xkeban (generous, disliked by the village); xtabentun flowers grow on Xkeban's grave, foul tzacam thorn plants on Utz-colel's; Utz-colel returns as Xtabay and haunts the ceiba. Other versions: Wikipedia says she may turn into a serpent and devour men, or throw victims off cliffs; in Quintana Roo she punishes drunks, thieves and violent criminals. Yucatan Today adds a hypothesis (from one teacher) that colonial priests reshaped the ceiba into a symbol of evil; Wikipedia treats this as only suggested.

Size figures vary: 20-25 m typical (INPI), 20-40 m (Mexico Desconocido), up to 60.4 m verified (Wikipedia), 70 m claimed (several). Use 'taller than most trees / as tall as a ten-storey building or more' only if hedged.

maya_terms.meaning: the ceiba, Ceiba pentandra; literally 'green tree' / 'first tree' (ya'ax = green or first, che' = tree)

the underworld, reached by the ceiba's roots (INPI, mayan.org); Yucatan Today pairs it with the name Mitnal - hedge, and keep it light

legendary female spirit linked to the ceiba; spellings vary by source

cautions: Religion and death: Xibalba is the realm of the dead, the INPI text makes the west (black) ceiba 'the place where the dead rest', and the Xtabay legend involves death and seduction. For a beginner family story say only 'the roots go down to the underworld, the trunk is our world, the branches reach the sky', with no mention of the dead or of gods.

Present the ceiba's sacredness as a living tradition ('many people in Maya villages consider it sacred and treat it with respect'), not as a fact about all Maya, and avoid saying people 'worship' the tree. The sources speak of respect, thanks and ceremonies.

Do not say every village has a ceiba in the plaza or that ceibas are 'never' cut. Say 'in many villages'; INPI itself describes thanking the tree before cutting, and a 2025 report describes a ceiba being damaged in a plaza in Ciudad del Carmen, Campeche.

Avoid the Xtabay legend in a beginner story: it is folklore with adult themes (the sisters' sexuality, death, a spirit that lures and may kill men), versions vary a lot, and one source says the sinister meaning may be a colonial-era reshaping. If used at all, keep to one hedged line ('some grandparents tell of a spirit in the legends') or omit.

Avoid the INPI creation myths (wooden people made from ceiba wood; Tepeu and Kukulkan as creator gods; Lacandon myth of children born from ceiba roots): they appear in one source only, mix Popol Vuh (K'iche') and Yucatec material, and Lacandon is not Yucatec. In the Popol Vuh as commonly told the wooden people are not described as made of ceiba - I did not verify this in the sources; treat it as an unresolved conflict.
Avoid the Xocen ceiba fall (4 Aug 2024) and its 'end of times' prophecy: reported by news only, hedged ('se piensa'), and frightening for children.

Four coloured ceibas: popular sites attribute them to the Popol Vuh, which is unconfirmed (Popol Vuh is K'iche'); the Yucatec Chilam Balam books are the more likely colonial Yucatec source, but I did not find the passage. Knowlton and Vail (2010) argue the term yax cheel cab is a colonial hybrid concept. Use at most 'people say there are ceibas at the four corners of the world' and drop colours and meanings.
Number of heavens (13) and Mitnal/Xibalba pairing come from tourism/popular sources only; skip.
Do not use 'ceiba means green tree': INPI says so, but 'green tree' is the gloss of the Maya name ya'axche'. The Spanish word ceiba is not Maya (its origin was not checked in these sources).
No source found ties aluxes (forest guardian spirits) to the ceiba; do not link them in this story.

Source quality: strongest are INPI (government), CICY (research centre), the Bolles dictionary and Knowlton and Vail (academic, abstract only); Wikipedia, Posta and Por Esto are secondary; Yucatan Today, Mexico Desconocido and mayan.org are popular with little or no citation and were used only for corroboration.
Safety and tone: the trunk can be very spiny, so do not have children climbing the ceiba in the story; keep the tone respectful and avoid exoticising ('magic powers').
Poetic claims (quetzals and hummingbirds in the canopy, the wind god's music in the branches) come from a poem in the INPI book; use as imagery only.
